prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 800 words of John Snow's investigation of the 1854 cholera outbreak around Broad Street in London. The reader is a general reader with no medical background.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.

text:
In the last days of August 1854, cholera broke out in Soho, a crowded and poor district of London, and within about ten days more than five hundred people living within a few streets of one another had died. Cholera is an infection of the gut that drains the body of water so quickly that a healthy adult can go from well to dead in a day, and in the middle of the nineteenth century nobody knew what caused it. The accepted explanation was miasma, the belief that disease rose from foul air given off by rotting waste, filthy streets and polluted ground, and since Soho certainly smelled bad, the explanation seemed to fit what anyone could see and smell.

John Snow, a physician who lived a few streets away, did not accept it. He was best known for his work on anaesthesia, having administered chloroform to Queen Victoria during a childbirth, and he was a careful, abstemious, rather solitary man who liked measuring things. Years earlier, during the epidemic of 1848 and 1849, he had reasoned that cholera must be swallowed rather than breathed, because it struck the intestines first and the lungs not at all, and he had published a short book arguing that it travelled in the water people drank. Few were persuaded. In 1853 and 1854 he had gathered further support by comparing households in south London that were supplied by two water companies, one of which drew its water from the Thames upstream of the city's sewage while the other took it from a stretch fouled by it, and he found that deaths were far more common in the houses served by the dirtier source. That comparison was a strong piece of evidence, but it was statistical and spread across a huge area, and when the Soho outbreak began he saw a chance to test his idea in a place small enough to examine house by house.

He began by finding out where the dead had lived. Working from the registrar's lists of deaths and then walking the streets himself, knocking on doors and asking what the families had drunk, he marked each death on a map of the neighbourhood with a small bar, so that the deaths stacked up along the street frontage of the houses where they occurred. The bars clustered around the water pump in Broad Street, which was one of the main sources of drinking water for the area, and the nearer a household lay to that pump the more bars it carried. This alone proved little, since people who lived close together also breathed the same air, so Snow turned to the exceptions, which are often where an argument is won or lost. The workhouse in Poland Street, with hundreds of inmates in the middle of the affected area, lost only five, and Snow found that it had its own well and never needed the Broad Street pump. The Lion Brewery on the same street lost none of its workers, who were given beer as part of their pay and had a well of their own on the premises. Meanwhile, at the other end of the pattern, a widow living in Hampstead, miles from Soho, died after her son had been sending her bottles of water from the Broad Street pump because she preferred the taste, and a niece who drank some of it died as well, while nobody else in Hampstead fell ill.

On 7 September Snow took his findings to the Board of Guardians of the parish of St James, the local body in charge of such matters, and urged them to take the handle off the pump so that nobody could draw water from it. They agreed to do so the next day, a decision that required some faith in a man who had no official standing and no microscope evidence to show them. The epidemic was by then already in decline, partly because many residents had fled the district, so it is impossible to say how many lives the removal of the handle saved, and later accounts that credit it with ending the outbreak overstate what it did.

The explanation still lacked a source, and it was supplied in large part by a local clergyman, the Reverend Henry Whitehead, who had begun by doubting Snow's theory and set out to disprove it. Whitehead knew the families of the parish and carried out his own inquiries among them, and he eventually learned that a five-month-old girl living at 40 Broad Street had fallen ill with diarrhoea just before the outbreak began and had died in early September. Her mother had washed the child's soiled napkins and thrown the water into a cesspool in front of the house, and when the cesspool and the well were later dug up, investigators found that the drain was cracked and only a few feet from the well, so that the contents could have seeped straight into it. Whitehead came round to Snow's view and the two men ended up reporting the matter together.

The authorities were not moved. The General Board of Health reported that it saw no reason to accept that the pump water was responsible, and the pump handle was soon replaced. Snow died in 1858, aged forty-five, still regarded by most of his colleagues as a respectable doctor with a mistaken notion, and only in the following decades, as bacteriologists identified the cholera organism and public health officials built sewers that kept waste out of drinking water, did his reasoning come to be recognised as the foundation of modern epidemiology.
